text:
It gave her an inward start, and she felt a kind of shame, but it passed at once.

Without making the slightest movement, she answered:

“Yes, it came while you were lying ill with fever.”

He tenderly patted her head. “And so you read the letter? You had to, of course. My poor sweet Conny.”

“I thought it concerned business matters that required an answer.”

“Naturally, naturally,” he said gently.

“I shall fetch it for you.” She was about to rise.

“Oh no, wait a little, sit still. I want to talk to you. Lay your head back again.”

“I would rather sit upright; I hear better then.”

He held her hand in both of his. “Have you taken this to heart, my little Conny?”

She did not answer.

“Have you taken it to heart?” he repeated, kissing her hand.

She made a quick sideways movement with her head and said resentfully: “There is no use discussing it. I would rather be spared.”

“You must not think of it any more, must not let it disturb your love. There is no reason for that. This lies behind us. We have nothing to do with it.”

She had drawn away from him and now sat in a slanting posture, her hand under her cheek and her elbow on the table. The lamplight fell on one side of her face. It was pale, and around her mouth there was an indefinably complex expression: pain and a little mockery, defiance and shyness, aversion and something of hardened determination.

“You know, Constance,” he continued softly, “that men do not live chastely, cannot, ought not to do so. And surely, Constance, you did not enter into our marriage with mistaken notions on this point.”

She sat utterly motionless. He waited for her to say something.

“It is so strange to sit here and talk and not receive a single word in reply. Have you nothing to say, Constance?”

She made a warding-off gesture with her hand. “I hear what you are saying,” she said, “and there is nothing to answer.”

“These casual liaisons that young men enter into with one girl or another,” Lorck continued after a little while, “not to mention purely sexual intercourse, are in reality of little significance—indeed, as far as the latter is concerned, of no significance whatever. It is self-defence, a surrogate, if you will, and has not the slightest effect upon a man’s ability later to feel a true love.” He stopped and stroked her from the shoulder down over her arm, slowly and cautiously, many times. “Do you not understand that this is so, Constance?”

She made the same warding-off gesture as before.

“We think so differently about this,” she said. “Yes, that is to say, you cannot understand what it is like for me.” She suddenly burst into tears.

He let her weep. It lasted only a minute or two. Then she sat motionless as before.

“But it is irrational, unreasonable, foolish,” he said, a little impatiently. “If you do not get the better of this, it may utterly ruin our life, and I should think you ought to be a little careful about that.”

The former strange expression appeared around her mouth, and she raised her eyebrows slightly.

“Do you not believe that I possess the full ability to love you, Constance? Do you not believe that I love you as deeply as it is possible to do?” he asked insistently.

“I do not know,” she answered in a weary tone.

“So you do not know!” He suddenly rose. His voice was completely changed. “Then I can at least assure you that you have received a love as fresh and good as you could wish it to be.”

She answered nothing. In silence he paced up and down the floor several times.

Then he knelt on a stool at her feet and took her hands between his.

“I understand that it has hurt you, my Conny—now I comprehend your changed manner, and it is a relief to me, for surely this is something that can be remedied. Oh, Constance—you do not know how I have suffered. I have been unhappy, jealous—imagine it, jealous!” He kissed her hands and looked up at her for an answer, but she did not open her mouth.

“A stone has fallen from my heart,” he continued. “The moment I could read the connection on your face, my sorrow was gone. Yes, for surely, Constance, you will not think of the past, but of the future; it is yours. You know how I longed for you, how weary I was of everything else. With you begins, as I have so often said, my real life.—You must not feel aversion towards me because of an illusion.”

“I feel no aversion,” she said tonelessly.

“But what is it, then? Why are you not as you were before?”

“Because it has become so different. The joy in your love is gone. It has withered and can never flower again. That is what has happened. Nothing else.”

“But it shall return—I shall not give up until I have loved it forth again. It shall become greater and truer than before.”

He rose and was about to press a kiss upon her mouth. She inclined her head slightly to one side, so that he reached only her cheek.

“Are you avoiding my caresses? Do you not like me to kiss you?”

She had risen and stood before him with her arms hanging down and her gaze averted. If only he would stop—this examination was far too unpleasant, she thought.

“Oh yes,” she said in a low voice, “just kiss me as much as you wish.”

He turned quickly and went into the bedroom, where she heard him undress and go to bed.

Constance remained for a long time leaning back on the sofa, her arms crossed over her breast. She thought of Lorck’s calm self-assurance, his confidence that everything would come right so long as there was nothing amiss with him and his love, his inability to understand the simple fact that she had ceased to love him. But before she knew it, she was sitting there going over her conversation with Mejer; she smiled faintly when it dawned upon her that she was much more preoccupied with him than with this matter concerning Lorck. She was glad that it was so, for the torment she had suffered at first was not to be endured. What a fascinating man Mejer was—the resonance of his voice, and that smile which came so rarely and lit up every corner of his face; how enchanting that smile was. What would it not be to be loved by him.... She closed her eyes and covered her face with her hands—it was burning hot, and her temples were throbbing.
